title: Grade 5 Science — Mon, Jun 23
description: Nervous System and Sense Organs — Day 1 of 5: The brain
subject: science

questions.question: The nervous system is the body's communication network. Which organs make up the CENTRAL nervous system?
questions.explanation: The Central Nervous System (CNS) = Brain + Spinal cord. They receive, process and send messages throughout the body. The peripheral nervous system = all the nerves outside the CNS.

questions.question: The brain is divided into three main parts. Which part is responsible for THINKING, memory, language and voluntary movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain — responsible for thinking, reasoning, memory, language, emotions and voluntary (conscious) movements. It is divided into left and right hemispheres.

questions.question: Which part of the brain controls BALANCE and coordination of movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum (at the back/base of the brain) controls balance, posture and coordination. Walking in a straight line, riding a cycle — all require the cerebellum.

questions.question: The medulla oblongata controls which vital functions?
options: Breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure — all involuntary (automatic) functions
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata (brainstem) controls involuntary, life-sustaining functions: breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing. These continue even when you are asleep.

questions.question: The brain is protected by the skull (cranium). What fluid further cushions it inside?
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord inside the skull/vertebral column. It acts as a shock absorber, protecting against impact.

questions.question: A student learns a new dance move. After much practice, they do it automatically without thinking. Which part of the brain is now more involved?
options: None — the body moves without the brain
questions.explanation: Initially, learning a new movement involves the cerebrum (conscious thinking). With practice, the cerebellum takes over to make the movement smooth and automatic. This is motor learning.

questions.question: The brain has two hemispheres (left and right). Generally, which side controls the left side of the body?
options: The spinal cord decides which side
questions.explanation: The brain is contralateral — the RIGHT hemisphere controls the LEFT side of the body, and vice versa. This is called crossed lateralisation.

questions.question: A person suffers a stroke (blood supply interrupted) in the left hemisphere. What might they lose?
options: Speech and right-side movement (left hemisphere controls language and right side of body)
questions.explanation: Left hemisphere = language/speech + controls right side of body. Left hemisphere stroke → difficulty speaking (aphasia) + right-side weakness/paralysis. Brain areas have specific functions.

questions.question: Why is the brain so heavily protected (skull + meninges + CSF)?
options: The brain is the control centre of the entire body — damage is irreversible since most brain cells cannot regenerate; maximum protection is essential
Protection makes the brain work faster
The skull is the same as other bones — no special protection
questions.explanation: Most brain neurons cannot regenerate (unlike skin cells). Brain damage = permanent loss of function. The triple protection (skull + membranes + fluid) reflects the brain's critical, irreplaceable role.

questions.question: Which part of the brain would be active when you are ASLEEP?
options: The medulla — it keeps breathing and heartbeat going even during sleep
No part of the brain works during sleep
questions.explanation: The medulla controls involuntary functions that never stop (breathing, heartbeat). During sleep, cerebrum activity reduces but the medulla (and other brainstem parts) remain fully active to keep you alive.

questions.question: Brain cell is called a neuron. What is special about neurons compared to most other cells?
options: They have very long extensions (axons) to transmit electrical signals over long distances, and most cannot divide/regenerate
questions.explanation: Neurons have a cell body + long axon (can be over 1m long in motor neurons) + dendrites. The axon conducts electrical impulses at up to 120 m/s. Unlike skin cells, neurons rarely regenerate — damage is often permanent.

questions.question: A person with a damaged cerebellum would have trouble with:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar damage → ataxia: unsteady gait, poor coordination, trembling. They can still think (cerebrum), breathe (medulla), and see (visual cortex) — but smooth, coordinated movement is impaired.

questions.question: The hypothalamus (a small area of the brain) controls hunger, thirst and body temperature. Which broad brain region contains it?
options: Cerebrum (specifically, the diencephalon below the cerebral hemispheres)
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus sits beneath the cerebral hemispheres (in the diencephalon/forebrain region). It regulates hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep cycles and links the nervous system to the hormonal system.

questions.question: Three brain parts in order of evolutionary age (oldest to newest) approximately:
options: Medulla (oldest, basic survival) → Cerebellum (movement) → Cerebrum (newest, thinking)
All three evolved at the same time
questions.explanation: The brainstem/medulla is the oldest (found in reptiles, fish — basic survival). Cerebellum is older (movement coordination). Cerebrum is most recently evolved and most developed in humans — allows complex thought, language, culture.

questions.question: Match brain part to function: Cerebrum → ___, Cerebellum → ___, Medulla → ___
questions.explanation: Cerebrum = thinking, memory, language, voluntary actions. Cerebellum = balance, coordination. Medulla = breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure (involuntary, life-sustaining functions).
